en: The Hymn of One Hundred and Eight Names of Śrī Śaṅkarācārya Śrī Śaṅkarācārya, the most excellent teacher, is the bestower of the bliss of Brahman;
he is the sun that dispels the darkness of ignorance and the moon for the ocean of sublime knowledge. (1)
The establisher of the system of castes and stages of life, the illustrious bestower of liberation, devoted to instructing his disciples, and the granter of the desires of his devotees. || 2 ||

He knows the secrets of the subtle reality, he awakens others to what ought and ought not to be done; with his hand adorned by the *jñānamudrā*, he removes the suffering from the hearts of his disciples. || 3 ||
The uprooter of the hermitage of wandering mendicants, whose intellect was independent of all other systems,
the teacher who established non-duality, he was the very embodiment of Śaṅkara himself.

He was the preceptor who established the six systems of philosophy, the illuminator of the path of the three Vedas, the knower of the truth of the Vedas and Vedānta, and the crusher of the doctrines of evil disputants. || 5 ||
Devoted to dispassion, peaceful, a deliverer from the ocean of saṃsāra,
with a lotus-face ever serene, he is the illuminator of the ultimate truth.
He is a knower of the essence of the Purāṇas and Smṛtis, eternally contented, great, and pure;
he is perpetual bliss, free from fear, unattached, and of stainless nature.
Free from possessiveness and free from ego, his lotus feet are worshipped by the universe;
he is the essence of pure being, preeminent in goodness, and radiant with qualities beyond counting.
He is sinless, the heart of Arha, the bestower of wisdom and eloquence,
whose self is truth, who is of virtuous character, and who is distinct from the systems of Sāṅkhya and Yoga.
A mass of austerity and great splendor, he knows the divisions of the three qualities;
he is the destroyer of the Kali age, a knower of time and action, and the warder-off of the quality of darkness (tamas).

The Blessed One, the conqueror of Bhāratī, the scholar invoked as Śāradā, the knower of the distinction between dharma and adharma, and the demonstrator of the differentiation of the targets. || 11 ||

The yogi is a master of the arts of *nāda* and *bindu*, a sun within the lotus of the heart, a treasury of supersensuous knowledge, and one who possesses the discernment between the eternal and the non-eternal. (12)
The self whose nature is consciousness and bliss, who effects entry into the body, who is rich in superhuman conduct, the bestower of security, and the source of forgiveness. (13)

He is the capable one, the bestower of auspiciousness, of vast majesty, and the delighter of the universe; he is self-luminous, the eternal support, the kinsman of all, and the source of well-being. || 14 ||
Possessing vast renown, a lord of speech, and ever eager for the welfare of all the worlds, he arrived at the journey to Kailāsa as a worshiper of the Moon-crested Lord. || 15 ||
In Kāñcī, he was initiated into the installation of the Yantra known as the Śrīcakra-rāja;
his heart’s desire was fulfilled by the Mother, who was pleased by his ear-ornament consisting of the Śrīcakra. || 16 ||
The author of works such as the Brahmasūtra-Upaniṣad-bhāṣya, the establisher of the four Vedas in the four directions, he was possessed of great intelligence. || 17 ||
The destroyer of the seventy-two schools, the lord who has conquered all directions, clad in saffron robes, his body smeared with ashes. (18)
Richly endowed with the single staff consisting of wisdom, with a water-pot shining in his hand, he was the preceptor of the circle of great teachers, known by the name Bhagavatpāda. || 19 ||
Delighted by the vision of Vyāsa, the lord of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga’s city composed many hymns, chief among them being the Saundaryalaharī. || 20 ||
He was a master of the sixty-four arts, a nourisher of Brahma-rākṣasas,
known by the illustrious name Maṇḍanamiśra, and highly praised by his own brother Jaya.
He who was worshipped by Toṭakācārya, whose feet were honored by Padmapāda, and who bestowed the knowledge of Brahman upon Hastāmalaka, the lord of yogins. || 22 ||
He was the bestower of the stage of renunciation upon his excellent disciple named Sureśvara;
he was a devotee of Nṛsiṃha and a worshipper of Heramba, who is filled with excellent jewels. || 23 ||
The sovereign of the lion-throne of exposition, worshiped by the world, the teacher of the world—thus [ends the praise] of the illustrious Śaṅkarācārya, the supreme teacher of all the worlds. 24.
Whoever recites with devotion the one hundred and eight names at the three junctions of the day shall obtain all desires, which bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the hymn of the one hundred and eight names of the venerable Śaṅkarācārya.
